text: The recycler has a bale of plastic ready to ship and the buyer backs out. Where does {name} expect that bale to go?
author: Codex writer B

text: It'll stay at the plant until somebody wants it, {presiding}. I'd still put a refund on the bottle. Right now there's nothing in it for the person who picks it up off the ground.
author: Codex writer B

text: Getting a bottle off the roadside is worth doing, {presiding}. Selling the material takes a buyer.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want the buyer's name before sending a load over there, {presiding}. If the sale falls through, the recycler has to find another bay in the warehouse.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's where I get stuck, {first}. The customer can collect the refund while the recycler still has a bale nobody will buy.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where would {name} put the first bag of returns in a grocery that barely has room for the stock it sells?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask whether the shop can share a return counter with a neighbor, {presiding}. I'd vote for the deposit and give a small store somewhere to send the empties.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd take {first} into the stockroom with the owner. If there's space for those bags between deliveries, the owner can show us where.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have to move something out to make room, {presiding}. I'd count what the shop gives up before voting yes.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd walk through that stockroom with {first} and ask the owner what would have to come out. Until I see the space, I can't promise it's there.
author: Codex writer B

text: The students have been collecting bottles for their trip. What would {name} tell the club treasurer those bottles will bring once the refund ends?
author: Codex writer B

text: Get a price from the scrap yard, {presiding}. A club could still collect cans after repeal, but I'd hate to see the treasurer book a bus on the old refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: They'd lose the deposit income, {presiding}. I favor repeal, but I wouldn't promise those students their cans will bring the same money.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund, {first}. A treasurer who counts the bottles today can tell the class what they'll have for the trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the club bring its receipts in, {presiding}. Before taking the refund away I'd like the committee to see what that money bought last term.
author: Codex writer B

text: The grocer paid the last customer on time. How long does the store have to get its own money back, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the grocer a filing date of its own, {presiding}. A clerk could pay a customer on the last afternoon and still need time to send the claim in.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give the stores a chance to settle up, {presiding}. They need time to file after the last customer brings a bottle back.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's the date I'd want in writing, {first}. The shopper has already been paid. The grocer shouldn't have to get a truck there that same day to recover the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can't give {first} a date the dealer can rely on. That's why I'd keep the deposit until we know how those last claims will be paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: These drinks sit beside each other on the shelf. If only one carries a deposit, what can the cashier show the customer, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Mark the bottle, {presiding}. Then the clerk can turn it in their hand and point out the refund without calling a manager.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with what the shopper can see, {presiding}. If the label tells the drinks apart, put the refund there too.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put me at that counter with {first} and I couldn't explain why one counts and the other doesn't. I'd settle the list before handing the cashier the job.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd send the list back to committee, {presiding}. By the time the lid comes off, the shopper should already know what the empty bottle is worth.
author: Codex writer B

text: The distributor marks the bottles and the clerk counts them when they come back. Which of those jobs would {name} pay a handling allowance for?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd pay the store for taking returns, {presiding}. Let the distributor include the cost of marking the cases in what it charges to deliver them.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let both bring in their costs, {presiding}. Marking a case takes different work from counting loose bottles at the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Show {first} what happens behind the counter when a bag comes in. Somebody has to count it, sort it and put it somewhere. I'd price that work before promising an allowance.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with the clerk who sorts the bottles, {presiding}. If the distributor wants a share too, I'd ask what work the store hasn't already done.
author: Codex writer B

text: Say I pay the deposit on my way home tonight and the refund ends tomorrow. What happens when I finally empty the bottle, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd let {first} bring that empty back. Set a final return day far enough out to finish the drink, and put it up on the shelf while people are still buying.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd stop charging the deposit on new sales and keep the return counter open for the old bottles, {presiding}. Those shoppers have already paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: Finish the drink and take the bottle back, {first}. That's the promise the store made at the till, and it's one reason I'd keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the store can take my deposit Friday and turn me away Saturday, {presiding}, I'm voting to keep the return counter open.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where would {name} send a family with a box of glass if the store stops taking returns and the town leaves glass at the curb?
author: Codex writer B

text: A county drop-off might take them, {presiding}. Before we print directions, let's find out which sites actually handle glass.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have each county name the site that will take the glass, {presiding}. Read those names against the list of towns and see who would be left without one.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want to give {first} directions from the grocery to a place that actually takes glass. Right now a family can get that job done when they buy food.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the store counter, {presiding}. Until somebody can name a nearby place that takes glass, we're sending that family home with the same box.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll support {bill}. Let distributors pick up each other's empties so the grocer can clear the stockroom in one trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm with the member, {presiding}. Let's hear from the corner shops about where a shared return counter could go.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put the refund on the label and let people collect what they paid. That's what I'd vote for in {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can't support {bill} until we know who pays when a different distributor takes the empty back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Stand behind a customer with a sack of cans and one clerk at the till, {presiding}. That's why I'm voting no.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give the bottlers until next session to bring us a litter plan before I voted for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I share that doubt, {presiding}. I'd want to see a buyer for the plastic before asking stores to collect it this way.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm on the same side. Before we send {bill} on, I'd like a bottler to show us the return trip on a map.
author: Codex writer B

text: Counting and sorting take paid time. Who covers those wages under {bill}? Until the grocer has an answer, my vote is no.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd support {bill} with a refund you can collect wherever that kind of drink is sold. Who remembers where they bought a soda?
author: Codex writer B

text: If the coverage in {bill} is confusing, fix the label. That's a poor reason to give up on the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give {issue} a chance. Could the distributors share a pickup so the store doesn't have to wait on each truck?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end it too, {presiding}. A grocer could use that room for groceries again.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll vote for {bill}. I'm reserving judgment on when a shop should have to file its last claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, end the deposit. I'd give people time under {bill} to bring back bottles they've already paid on.
author: Codex writer B

text: Until you can tell a family where else to take glass on a grocery trip, I'm voting against {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep it, {presiding}. A club collecting cans can count on the refund when it plans a field trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: Why throw the refund out? I'd hear an amendment to {bill} to pay stores for handling bottles.
author: Codex writer B

text: I agree, {presiding}. Someone who paid the deposit ought to decide when to bring the bottle back.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm wary of {bill} taking the store out of the picture. A county site can be a long drive.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund too, {presiding}. A bag of cans is worth carrying home when you know what you'll get for it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd let the shopkeeper have the stockroom back. I'm voting for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: We can stop charging on new bottles and still honor the old ones. On those terms I'd support {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end the refund, {presiding}, and ask which county sites take glass. I'd want those addresses posted before the last return day.
author: Codex writer B

text: That would help the grocers. Under {bill}, who credits the shop when the bottles go back on somebody else's truck? I'd have the distributors agree on that.
author: Codex writer B

text: For {bill} I'd invite a shop owner to walk us through that trip. A shared counter needs to be somewhere customers can reach.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. A parent buying juice ought to be able to tell right there in the aisle what the empty is worth.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a settlement between distributors answer that objection to {bill}? A customer can't tell which truck brought the bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: Then let's hear how many empties a small shop can take at once. I'd like the clerk to have an answer under {bill} besides turning everybody away.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose we put {bill} off. What would you do next session if the bottlers just ask for more time?
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the recycler bring the purchase order, {first}. A picture of the plastic piled up outside won't tell us whether anybody has agreed to take it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd put the trip back to the filling plant on that map, {presiding}. An empty takes up room on a truck too.
author: Codex writer B

text: Exactly, {presiding}. A store can't make payroll with the deposit it hands back to a customer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who settles with a shop that pays out on a brand it never stocked? That's the part I'd want written into {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which drinks would earn that mark under {bill}? The label comes after somebody has made that choice.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would that truck take everybody's bottles on the same day, {presiding}? A grocer needs to know when the space will be clear.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. If we pass {bill}, that room is worth something to the store even if it never sells another bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: Fair enough. Before fixing a deadline in {bill}, I'd hear from the people who check the claims.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd put the last return date under {bill} on the store door while people still have time to bring their bottles in.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose the county took glass at the grocery, {first}. Would that answer your objection to repeal, or do you want the shopper to get the deposit back as well?
author: Codex writer B

text: What would the scrap yard pay the club? I'd like to see that beside the refund before we decide what {bill} means for those trips.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who would pay the handling allowance under {bill}? I'd hate to tell a shopkeeper we've settled it when nobody can say who writes the check.
author: Codex writer B

text: A family that buys drinks by the case may still have full bottles on the shelf when {bill} takes effect. Thank you for bringing them up.
author: Codex writer B

text: How far is the round trip from the edge of the county, {presiding}? That's what I'd put beside the address.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's why I'd vote against {bill}. A kid picking up cans shouldn't need to follow the scrap market to know whether the trip is worth it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a regular pickup clear enough room for that shopkeeper? I'd try it before voting for {bill} to end every customer's refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Once {bill} takes effect, how will the clerk tell an old bottle from one sold after the change if the packages still look alike?
author: Codex writer B

text: Post the address, {presiding}, but walk the route before you send anyone there. How is a shopper on foot supposed to carry glass from the grocery to the county site?
author: Codex writer B

text: Give an empty can a refund and a school club can collect it for the trip fund. The club can work out what a bag is worth before anybody goes knocking. That's why I'm voting for {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, a grocer has every right to ask who'll take the bottles away. Distributors can share that pickup. I want us to make the return trip work, and I'll vote for the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: When you pay a deposit, you ought to be able to walk back into a store with your empties and get it back. That's the promise I'd vote to make with {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: If we put a deposit on a drink, somebody buying it ought to know at the shelf whether they can claim a refund. I support {bill-name}, and I want that clear before the first bottle comes back.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, imagine running a corner grocery. Where would you put a day's worth of returns while you wait for a truck? That space has to come from somewhere. I'll vote against {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A grocer can mark the minutes a clerk spends counting bottles. What goes on the distributor's claim? I'd hold my vote, {presiding}, until I see what we're paying each of them to do.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can see how a bottle gets from the store to the recycler. What happens if the recycler has a warehouse full and no buyer for the plastic? I can't support {bill-name} with that question open.
author: Codex writer B

text: Look at the drink cases the way a cashier sees them, {presiding}. Same size bottle, same cap. If only one carries a refund, I'd want the cashier to have something to go by besides the flavor.
author: Codex writer B

text: Consider a grocer who stores returns in the stockroom. I'd give the owner that space back. That's a reason I'm voting for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I favor ending the deposit. Before we finish with {bill}, I want the grocer who pays the last customer a refund to know where to send the claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: We can end the deposit and still give people time to bring back the bottles they paid it on. I'll support {bill} and press for a last return date people can plan around.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for repeal, {presiding}. A family with a box of glass will still need somewhere to take it. I'd like the collection arrangements in people's hands before the refunds end.
author: Codex writer B

text: If a school club pays for trips with cans, what do we tell the kids when {bill} takes their refund away? They'd have to start by asking what a scrap dealer would pay. I'd keep the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: A refillable already has a long trip back to the plant to be washed. Why pass {bill} and take away the refund that gets it as far as the counter? I'm voting against repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think about the bottles in somebody's pantry, {presiding}. They paid the deposit at the register. I don't want their chance to get it back to depend on whether they hear about the cutoff. I'm against repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper can walk a bag of bottles back to the corner store. If {bill} leaves a collection site outside town, how does somebody without a car get there? I want to keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the grocer and the driver lay their costs side by side. I favor {bill}, and I want the people who do the work to have a say in how we divide the handling money.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like a bottler who can wash and refill a bottle to have a chance at getting it back. The refund in {bill} gives somebody at home a reason to carry it to the store. My vote is yes.
author: Codex writer B

text: At the register a customer ought to be able to ask which drinks carry the deposit and get a straight answer. I think we can manage that. I ask the chamber to pass {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: If a shop has room for groceries or empties, let's find it a partner for returns. I'd work on the collection arrangements in {bill} and vote to put a deposit on the bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: The bottlers say they can get the empties off the roadside themselves. Give them until we meet again, {presiding}. When we come back I want to see the road they picked.
author: Codex writer B

text: A clerk working alone can't leave the lunch line to count a customer's whole sack of cans. I'd need some leeway for the little stores, {presiding}, before I could vote for a deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: The water delivery routes overlap, {presiding}. A store could hand back money on another distributor's bottles all week. I'd want that store paid before I voted to start collecting deposits.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm looking at this from the loading dock, {presiding}. A driver with a mixed load ought to know whose empties can ride. I'd want that settled before stores have to start taking them.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd be glad to see the end of the argument at the counter over which bottle qualifies. I'll support {bill}. Give customers fair notice about the empties they already have.
author: Codex writer B

text: For the clerk alone at the register, a bag of empties is a job to do while the lunch line waits. That's who I've got in mind as I vote for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A refund brings back the plastic. It can't guarantee a buyer for what piles up at the recycling plant. I'd vote for {bill} to end the deposit and still want to know who's buying the material.
author: Codex writer B

text: I support repeal. A club that raises trip money with cans needs a straight answer about {bill}. The scrap dealer may pay less. The kids deserve to know that while there's still time to plan.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm willing to change what a store gets paid for handling returns. What {bill} ends is the customer's refund. That's where I part company with the sponsor.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who carries the cost of the last refund while a dealer waits for the distributor to settle up? I'd keep the deposit. If {bill} passes, I want that dealer's claim honored.
author: Codex writer B

text: If similar bottles get different treatment, let's clear up which ones qualify. A customer shouldn't have to give up a refund to get a clearer label. That's why I'm voting against {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd rather put the grocer and the distributor at this table, {presiding}, and hear what each trip costs. We can revisit their allowances and keep paying customers for bringing the containers back.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the recycler showed us a signed order for the plastic, would that satisfy {name}, or would the plant need a second buyer in case the order falls through?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want another outlet, {first}. One canceled shipment can leave the recycler renting room for bales it thought would be on the road by now.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let me see when the buyer can turn a shipment down, {presiding}. A signature doesn't clear the warehouse if slow sales let the customer cancel.
author: Codex writer B

text: The stockroom is a good place to start. What would you ask {hearing-opponent} about freeing up space while the refund is still in effect?
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether a shared pickup would clear enough room between deliveries. I'd put the same question to {hearing-supporter} and compare what each could find out from the grocers.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask for a pickup schedule from a shop that runs out of room. That would help us decide whether to change {bill-name} or leave it as filed.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you send the dealer's last claim to {hearing-opponent} to see where a store could get stuck waiting for its money?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. Ask {hearing-supporter} to follow the claim from the distributor's side. Have both mark where they'd expect to see a receipt.
author: Codex writer B

text: Use {bill-name} as it stands when you send it. If the store can't tell who settles its claim by reading the bill, we have more to write.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which part of the last refund would you ask {hearing-supporter} to trace for the committee?
author: Codex writer B

text: The handoff at the loading dock. Then let {hearing-opponent} check whether the count on the driver's ticket matches what the dealer paid out.
author: Codex writer B

text: The trip from the register to the reimbursement check. If there's a gap, I'd like it marked in the margin of {bill-name} before we vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before we set the last return day in {bill-name}, who would you ask to try it out with a bag of empties?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to take the shopper's part. Where would someone find the date on a bottle bought before repeal?
author: Codex writer B

text: Give {hearing-supporter} the receipt and the proposed date. See whether a person who bought the drinks last week would know how long they had.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you send the proposed notice to {hearing-opponent} before you settle on a deadline?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. I'd send it to {hearing-supporter} as well. I want to know what each thinks a cashier should do with a customer who shows up on the last afternoon.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, with the draft of {bill-name} beside it. Someone reading only the notice should get the same last return day as someone reading the bill.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you ask {hearing-supporter} to check where the glass could go before stores stop paying refunds?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, and I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to try those directions from a grocery store on foot. A site can take glass and still be out of reach for a shopper.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want the site operator to confirm what it takes. I wouldn't put a collection site into the notice for {bill-name} on the strength of a street address alone.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which sign would you show {hearing-opponent} first, the price on the shelf or the notice at the return counter?
author: Codex writer B

text: The shelf tag. I'd hand the return notice to {hearing-supporter} and ask them to read the signs together as a customer would.
author: Codex writer B

text: The return notice. If it says people have longer than {bill-name} actually allows, the cashier will have to answer for that at the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: The committee heard {hearing-supporter} on the bill. What would you want checked at the register before you promise the clerk a shorter line?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want a timed count with customers waiting. Let {hearing-opponent} pick the time of day so we're also hearing what happens when the shop is busy.
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether the work actually goes away under {bill-name} or just moves to the afternoon when everyone brings the last bags in.
author: Codex writer B

text: If a distributor offered to take the bags directly, what would you need from {hearing-opponent} before you called that a fair trade for shoppers?
author: Codex writer B

text: A trip somebody could actually make without a car. Then I'd ask {hearing-supporter} whether the distributor would be open when that person got there.
author: Codex writer B

text: Directions a customer could use after work. I'd want that arrangement confirmed before voting to replace returns at the store under {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose we hear from {hearing-opponent} again. What would convince you a recycler could sell the bottles coming back?
author: Codex writer B

text: A buyer willing to take the next delivery as well as what's already baled. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to read the cancellation terms with me.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want an order the recycler can ship against. I wouldn't change my vote on {bill-name} just because somebody found room to store more plastic.
author: Codex writer B

text: You've already said the club could get less for its cans. What would you ask {hearing-supporter} to bring back before the students set a trip price?
author: Codex writer B

text: A quote from the scrap yard for a load like the club's. I'd let {hearing-opponent} check that quote against what the club could collect in refunds now.
author: Codex writer B

text: An offer that says how long the price will hold. Before I support a deadline in {bill-name}, I want to know whether the club has time to collect and deliver the cans.
author: Codex writer B

text: What could we put in {bill-name} for a club that's collected the cans but hasn't turned them in yet?
author: Codex writer B

text: A final return period. I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to find out how much notice a sponsor needs to borrow a truck and get the bags to the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: A requirement to tell customers when the refund ends. I'd send {hearing-supporter} the proposed notice and ask where a student collecting cans would see it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Say the truck misses its last pickup. Who would you want to walk {hearing-supporter} through what stays on the grocer's floor?
author: Codex writer B

text: The receiver who signs for deliveries. I'd also invite {hearing-opponent} to see how much of that room the grocer gets back when the truck finally comes.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with whoever holds the key to that stockroom. The day {bill-name} takes effect and the day the grocer gets the space back could be a long way apart.
author: Codex writer B

text: A box of glass is heavy. Who would you put beside {hearing-opponent} to work out that trip home from the store and on to the collection site?
author: Codex writer B

text: Someone who walks to buy groceries. I'd have {hearing-supporter} meet them at the store so we're talking about the same trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: The person who picks the site. Before a notice goes out under {bill-name}, that person should see the route a shopper would have to take.
author: Codex writer B

text: A cashier may still have a line of people carrying old bottles. What would you put at the door so a shopper could sort the empties if {bill-name} passes?
author: Codex writer B

text: Pictures of the containers the store still takes. Give {hearing-opponent} a bottle from the shelf and see whether the sign tells them what to do with it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Try it with {hearing-supporter} carrying a bottle that looks like one we've covered but never had a deposit. That's the awkward conversation the cashier has to get right.
author: Codex writer B

text: What's the first thing a buyer could show {hearing-supporter} that we couldn't learn by looking at a stack of bales?
author: Codex writer B

text: A delivery date. If there's an order, {hearing-opponent} could check when the plastic is actually supposed to leave the building.
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether the buyer will take the next load too. If we're relying on that sale to make a case for changing {bill-name}, we need more than an empty corner in the warehouse.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like to hear where {hearing-supporter} would look for the last return date. What about the people who've already bought their bottles?
author: Codex writer B

text: Those bottles could sit in a garage for weeks. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to try finding the date from home before we settle on posting it in stores.
author: Codex writer B

text: The first time some people hear of {bill-name} could be when they bring the bottles back. I'd leave time between putting up the notice and closing the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Two empties on the counter, both from the same fridge. Where in {bill-name} could the clerk point to explain why only one pays?
author: Codex writer B

text: Read the labels. Could {hearing-supporter} match each drink to a line on our notice? That's what the clerk will have to do.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give {hearing-opponent} the two labels and the notice we're proposing. If you still have to know the answer in advance, the clerk doesn't stand a chance.
author: Codex writer B

text: If {hearing-opponent} brings back a brand the grocer has never stocked, does your notice tell the clerk to turn it away?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have the notice say which drinks still qualify. I'd want {hearing-opponent} to be able to read it without having to remember which store sold the bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: A brand list could shut somebody out by mistake. While returns are still open, {bill-name} ought to tell the clerk whether the kind of drink is what counts.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose the grocer honors that notice down to the last minute. When would {bill-name} let the grocer turn in the bottles?
author: Codex writer B

text: The customer should get the whole last day. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to follow the bottles from that last refund until the dealer can turn them over for payment.
author: Codex writer B

text: Two dates on the notice, please. I'd have {hearing-opponent} check which one a shopper would see first and print the dealer's instructions separately if it's confusing.
author: Codex writer B

text: What does a grocer do with another sack of empties when the truck is late, {presiding}? Something else has to come off the stockroom floor. That's why I'm voting to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give me a choice between a shelf for tomorrow's bread and a shelf for yesterday's bottles and I'll take the bread. That's my reason for supporting {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm backing {bill-name} for a pretty ordinary reason. A delivery driver ought to be able to get a hand truck through the back door without the clerk having to shift a stack of sticky bottles first.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, I'll vote to end the deposit. But who's holding the money when the last customer leaves? The shopper has a refund and the grocer has a bag of glass. We still owe that grocer a way to settle up.
author: Codex writer B

text: There's still some unfinished business on {bill}. Close the return counter, by all means. Keep the dealer's claim open long enough to get the money back into the till.

text: I support {bill-name}. A grocer who pays the last refund out of the register should be able to hand in the claim the next morning and get paid.

text: Picture somebody buying a case the evening before repeal. Under {bill}, I'd give that family time to drink it before they have to bring the bottles back. I'm ready to end the deposit on those terms.

text: Who has a bag of empties by the back door right now? People kept those bottles because we told them they'd get their money back. I'll support {bill-name} and a return period that keeps our word.

author: Codex writer B

text: Of course I'll vote for {bill-name}. But if the grocery quits taking glass on Monday, where do I carry it on Tuesday? A town ought to have an answer before its counter closes.
author: Codex writer B

text: A clerk shouldn't have to referee an argument over two bottles that look alike. I support repeal, {presiding}. Let's give the people who paid deposits on those bottles time to find out what's changing.
author: Codex writer B

text: Same size bottle, same shelf, different answer at the register. I'm voting for {bill} because I'd like to see that argument end. The shopper deserves to hear about the change before making a trip back.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for {bill-name}. I can see why a shopper would be sore about saving a bag of bottles and finding out at the counter that some of them never carried a deposit. Let's at least give people fair warning.

text: Think about a store with a single till, {presiding}. While the clerk is counting a sack of empties, the milk is sitting on the belt and nobody can pay for it. That's my vote for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who covers the register while the clerk sorts the bottles? At a little grocery the answer might be nobody. I'll vote for {bill} to get that clerk back to the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd support {bill-name} on the small store alone. A bag of returns arrives just as the lunch rush starts. Which customer is the only clerk supposed to keep waiting?
author: Codex writer B

text: Will somebody buy the next bale, {presiding}? Paying to get bottles back can fill a shed with plastic before there's a buyer ready to use it. That's why I can vote to end the deposit.

text: The refund gets a bottle as far as the plant. A buyer may need clean flakes, and all the plant has to sell is a bale. On that account I'm for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Line up a customer for the plastic and we've done something for recycling. Stack the bales in a warehouse and we've found a place to keep them. I'm supporting {bill-name} because a refund alone can't close that sale.
author: Codex writer B

text: A school club can count a refund before it books a bus, {presiding}. Scrap is worth what a buyer will pay that day, which may be less. I'm voting for repeal and I think the kids deserve to know that before they set the fare.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll vote for {bill}. Would I tell a club to keep collecting cans on the promise that the scrap will pay for the same trip? I wouldn't. They could come up short.

text: A bottler can send a truck back to the wash line with full cases of empties or with empty cases. It matters which, {presiding}. I'd keep the refund that gives the customer a reason to fill those cases.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm thinking of the grocer who's found a plant willing to refill the bottles. The truck can make that long trip only with what reaches the shop. I won't vote for {bill} to take away the reason for bringing the glass back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think of a family buying a case for company, {presiding}. They paid the deposit on every bottle. I'd leave them the refund even if the company comes later than they expected.
author: Codex writer B

text: A sign on the return counter won't reach a customer who's still drinking the first bottle. They paid on the whole case. I'm voting against {bill} because I want them to collect when the empties are ready.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who tells the person with full bottles in the pantry when the clock starts? I don't want {bill} to turn the refund they paid for into something they can miss between shopping trips. My vote is no.
author: Codex writer B

text: It's manageable to carry a few empties to the grocery and bring dinner home in the same bag. If {bill} sends the glass somewhere else, that shopper now has another trip to make on foot. I'd keep the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before giving up the refund, I'd like directions a person can actually follow with a box of bottles and no car. A county address alone doesn't get them there, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the grocery stops taking glass, which way does the shopper turn when they come out the door? They walked there. I'd want an answer that works on foot before I'd support {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd listen to a grocer who says the return counter costs more to run than the store gets paid. I can't tell that grocer that taking the customer's money away is the only answer. On {bill} I'll vote no.
author: Codex writer B

text: Bring me a change to the handling fee and I'll consider it, {presiding}. A shopper asking for the deposit back has kept their part of the bargain. I'd leave that part alone.
author: Codex writer B

text: What does a store need to do the work of taking bottles back? We can hear the answer without ending the refund. I'd separate those questions and vote against {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Follow the last empty across the counter. A customer gets paid today and the shop has to collect later. I'd keep the deposit, but if {bill} passes, don't close the grocer's books for them.
author: Codex writer B

text: The cash that leaves the drawer belongs to the customer. The grocer who advanced it still has a claim. I'd vote no on {bill}, and I'd protect that claim whichever way the vote goes.
author: Codex writer B

text: What happens when the distributor's truck turns up after the last return day? If the shop has already paid the customer, I want somebody to honor its claim, {presiding}. I'd keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Set the two bottles down with their labels facing the shopper. If you still can't tell which one pays, let's change what the label says. Throwing out the refund under {bill} seems a poor way to clear that up.
author: Codex writer B

text: A cashier ought to be able to explain the refund while the drinks are still on the shelf. Give the clerk a rule and a mark that match. I'd keep the refund and try that, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper brings back two empties from the same shelf and the clerk pushes one back across the counter. I'd ask which drinks we cover and how anyone could tell. I wouldn't start by voting for {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: The grocer makes room and counts what's brought in. The distributor has a route to cover. I'd hear the cost of each job before setting the allowances, {presiding}, and keep the customer's refund in place.
author: Codex writer B

text: How much of the expense happens behind the counter, and how much after the driver loads the cases? I'd want the grocer and the distributor to answer separately. Neither cost persuades me to pass {bill} and end the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the shop is paying someone to sort glass, let it show us the time involved. Then let the distributor bring in the pickup route. We can use both records to decide what the work is worth without passing {bill}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would {name} pay a grocer for counting returns even if the distributor got nothing for marking the packages?
author: Codex writer B

text: The store, yes. That clerk's on the clock the whole time. The distributor could bring the committee a printer's invoice if it wants an allowance too.
author: Codex writer B

text: What would {name} want written on the driver's pickup sheet before the truck leaves the yard?
author: Codex writer B

text: A list of the companies whose bottles can ride together. Then the grocer could get their cases ready before the truck pulls in.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the bottlers get that extra session, how would {name} tell whether their cleanup lasted?
author: Codex writer B

text: Go back after a busy weekend. If the ditch is full again, that tells us more than a photo from cleanup day.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would {name} let a small shop limit what each customer brings back in a day?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, and I'd post the limit where people park. Folks ought to know how much the store will take before they haul everything inside.
author: Codex writer B

text: What could the customer check before bringing those bottles back, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Look for the mark on the bottle itself. The carton might already be in the trash.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose the label tells the clerk the bottle carries a refund but nobody knows which truck brought it. Who would {name} send the claim to?
author: Codex writer B

text: The companies that sold the water could pay those claims out of a common account. Why send a clerk looking for a truck?
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with the store. I'd ask the distributor to bring in an invoice for changing the labels before it drew an allowance of its own.
author: Codex writer B

text: How would {name} find out what a return costs the shop on an ordinary afternoon?
author: Codex writer B

text: Stand at the counter with the owner. I'd time a return from the moment the clerk leaves the till until the empty is put away.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask the clerk to keep a slip by the register. Write down when a customer brings empties in and when the clerk can get back to selling groceries.
author: Codex writer B

text: A driver ought to be able to point to the cases the truck will take. If there's an exception, tell the store before it wheels the cases out.
author: Codex writer B

text: A grocer signs for the pickup and finds a stack of cases still on the dock. Whom should the grocer call, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: The dispatcher who sent that truck. I'd put that number on the pickup slip so the grocer doesn't have to go down a list of bottlers.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have the distributors who share the route give the store a single contact. The grocer shouldn't have to know which driver was meant to clear the dock.
author: Codex writer B

text: I want the road crew's account too. Ask the crew where it still has to stop and pull bottles out of the grass.
author: Codex writer B

text: What would make {name} bring the deposit proposal back when we next meet?
author: Codex writer B

text: If the bottlers come back with a cleanup day and nothing for the weeks after it, I'll ask for another hearing.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd walk that road with the people who mow it. If they're still stopping the mower to pick glass off the shoulder, I'd put the deposit back before the chamber.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the small shop post what it can take. A family with more than that should find out while it can still choose a different stop.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where does that leave someone who can only get a ride into town on Saturdays, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask which nearby store could take the whole load. A daily limit is a poor answer if the shopper has to hire another ride.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the grocer arrange a time for a big return. That Saturday customer could come when another clerk is there to cover the till.
author: Codex writer B

text: The refund ought to be legible on the empty container itself. A shopper won't always have a receipt from the store where it was bought.
author: Codex writer B

text: If somebody learns at the till that a bottle won't earn a refund, what should the cashier be able to show them, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: A matching pair with the marks visible. The customer should be able to see the difference without taking the cashier's word for it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep a guide to the marks beside the register. If the rule takes a manager to explain every time, the packaging still needs work.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the store one place to file. The distributors can work out their shares from their delivery records after the grocer gets paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would {name} make the shopper return the water bottle to the store that sold it?
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't. People buy water on the road and bring the empty home. I'd have the companies work out the route between them.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper saving an empty shouldn't have to save a receipt for it too. Let a store that takes the bottle claim the refund through the distributors.
author: Codex writer B

text: Watch a cashier take a bag of returns and you'll see where the store's allowance goes. I'm still looking for the distributor's part in that transaction, {presiding}. I'd send the payment provision back.
author: Codex writer B

text: There's a charge here for marking the packages. Before we agree to pay it, {presiding}, let the distributor bring in the bill for the labels and let the store bring in its payroll.
author: Codex writer B

text: The beer cases are out by the back door. The truck has room. Can the driver take a different company's empties? I'd settle that with the distributors before we tell stores to save every case, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Nobody at the register can move that stack of returns until a truck comes for it, {presiding}. Get the distributors to agree on who'll collect a mixed load and I'll take another look.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the bottlers the summer, {presiding}. Let them pick a stretch of road and keep it clear. When we come back, the highway crew can tell us how that went.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm willing to give the bottlers until next session to clean up the litter themselves, {presiding}. They ought to name the road now. Otherwise we'll come back to a fine photograph without knowing where it was taken.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose it's your turn at the lunch counter. The clerk sets your change down and starts counting a sack of cans. How long before you walk out? A corner store needs some say in how much it takes at once, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A grocery with help on every aisle can call someone up front for a big return. Try that in a shop where the only other person in the building is a customer, {presiding}. That's the store I worry about.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put an empty soda bottle beside an empty juice bottle and turn the labels away, {presiding}. Now ask a cashier to pay out on just one. I'd vote to start a deposit when there's a difference the cashier can show a shopper.
author: Codex writer B

text: The people writing this know which drinks qualify. The kid sent to the store with a bag of empties deserves to know too, {presiding}. I want something on the package that settles the question.
author: Codex writer B

text: A traveler buys a bottle of water on the highway and turns it in near home. The neighborhood grocer pays out. Which distributor owes the grocer? I'm waiting for that answer, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Follow an empty water bottle across town, {presiding}. The shopper can step across a delivery route without ever seeing a boundary. I'd like to know how the store on the far side gets its money back.
author: Codex writer B

text: The store has a payroll to meet. I'm with {name} on asking what we're buying before we promise anybody a handling fee.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the grocer bring a week's time sheets. That gives us something to compare the distributor's claim with.
author: Codex writer B

text: Right. The same person draws a wage whether there's a carton of milk on the counter or a sack of empties.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd send the allowance back to committee, {presiding}. A grocer and a bottler ought to be able to tell us separately what the work costs.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like them at the same table. Then we could ask whether both claims are charging us for the same job.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd make room at the hearing for the clerk who does the counting. A payroll sheet tells us what an hour costs. The clerk can tell us where it goes.
author: Codex writer B

text: Pay the store for counting bottles and take up the cost of labels when the distributors bring their receipts. I'd start the refund, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: What happens on the first delivery? A distributor who thinks we're paying for new labels could already have ordered them.
author: Codex writer B

text: Show me where the distributor has to bring its receipts before it gets paid. I could consider the store allowance on those terms.
author: Codex writer B

text: A manufacturer has to print the label anyway, {presiding}. I'd give the allowance to the counter clerk's employer and vote for the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: How much of that label run has already been printed? Changing a mark in the middle of a run could cost money.
author: Codex writer B

text: Then I'd want the allowance written that way. The grocer ought to know which part of the return work it covers.
author: Codex writer B

text: An empty truck could drive right past a grocer whose dock is stacked with cases. I'd wait to see the pickup agreement too, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Ask the store to initial the route sheet. That's how we'd find out whether anyone told the grocer which loads the driver can take.
author: Codex writer B

text: Exactly. And when the truck leaves cases behind, whose phone rings?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd wait with {name}. A driver shouldn't have to call different dispatchers from the dock to find out whether the cases can go.
author: Codex writer B

text: It's the grocer who has to stand there until somebody picks up. A dispatcher could settle that before the truck leaves.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the drivers themselves can read the agreement and tell us which loads they'd take, I'd be willing to hear it again.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the distributors share the route, {presiding}. A mixed load is a reason to pick up together, and I'd vote to start the deposit on that basis.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who takes the call when a distributor leaves the shared route? The grocer still has its cases on the dock.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like the drivers to know who's accepting the shared load before we ask a shop to stack it.
author: Codex writer B

text: A grocer could hand the driver a mixed pallet and get a signed pickup slip, {presiding}. I'd put that arrangement in the bill and vote yes.
author: Codex writer B

text: What goes on the slip if the driver takes half the pallet? That's the part I'd want the distributors to settle.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who keeps the pickup slip? I'd want the grocer to have a copy to point to when someone asks what happened to that load.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give the bottlers until we meet again, {presiding}. The people who pick up litter for a living can tell us whether the offer amounted to anything.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let's hear from the highway crew after the busy season. That's when I want the bottlers back here too.
author: Codex writer B

text: The crew could bring its regular pickup notes to the next hearing. No extra paperwork for anyone out on the road.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let them try the stretch they choose, {presiding}. I want that road named in the minutes so we're all looking in the same ditch next session.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll ask for the road name before we adjourn. Nobody should have to guess which stretch to visit later.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put the name in the minutes and the maintenance supervisor can check it against the crew's work orders.
author: Codex writer B

text: People buying these drinks today get nothing for returning the bottles. I'd start the refund now, {presiding}. The bottlers could still clean up the roadside this summer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would the bottlers still run the same trial? I'd like a chance to see what they can do on their own.
author: Codex writer B

text: I want to hear what happens on their stretch of road before we start taking deposits at every counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: The highway crew is already doing the pickup. Another season means more hours beside traffic. I'd rather give the people who empty the bottles a reason to bring them back, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: What does the crew think of letting the bottlers take over that stretch? I'd like the people doing the job to have a say.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's a fair question about the crew's hours. I'd ask the bottlers which days they'll send people out themselves.
author: Codex writer B

text: A sack beside the till can tie up the only cashier. Give the owner a say in how much the shop takes at once and I'll listen, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want that limit posted at the door. The clerk should be able to point to it before anybody empties a sack on the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Take me through a lunch rush at that counter. At what point does the owner have to ask someone to come back?
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't make a little market hire a second person just to get through the lunch line, {presiding}. I'd wait for a return rule the owner can manage.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like to hear what the owner does on the day someone brings in a trunkful. That's the day the rule has to work.
author: Codex writer B

text: When is there another pair of hands in the shop? I'd start with the clerk who has to call for help.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the small store post a daily limit and start the refund, {presiding}. A store with room and staff can keep taking the larger loads.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where can someone who tops that limit go? In a small town the other store could be a long drive.
author: Codex writer B

text: Show me that the corner shop can set the limit itself. I'd want the person who works the till involved.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd put the deposit in place and give a small store a way to schedule a large return, {presiding}. A shopper could come back when the clerk has help.
author: Codex writer B

text: What about a shopper whose ride can't come again? An appointment only helps if the person can get there.
author: Codex writer B

text: Post the hours by the door, then. It's a long walk home with the same sack you carried in.
author: Codex writer B

text: The person at the register shouldn't have to argue about which drink was in an empty bottle. I want a mark a customer can read too, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: It needs to stay readable after a trip home and back. I'd test it on the empty.
author: Codex writer B

text: Pass a sample down this row. Let's see who can find the refund mark without somebody pointing it out.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd hold this for a labeling rule, {presiding}. A customer ought to be able to separate the bottles at the kitchen sink.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's where I'd try reading it too. Nobody should need the carton the bottles came in.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd take the marked sample home and bring it back empty. If the mark's gone, we're still asking the clerk to guess.
author: Codex writer B

text: Print the refund on the container and start collecting it, {presiding}. A shopper can turn the bottle in their hand and see the mark.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where would the mark be on a clear bottle? I'd like to try it under the lights at a register.
author: Codex writer B

text: Has anybody brought a bottle off the filling line? I'd like to try reading the mark on one before we vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: We could show the qualifying mark on the shelf beside the price, {presiding}. Give the shopper that information at the sale and I'd support the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: The shelf is at the store. What would that shopper see when sorting bottles at home?
author: Codex writer B

text: Put the bottle beside the shelf sign. Can you tell from looking at both why the clerk paid on one bottle and turned the other away?
author: Codex writer B

text: If the neighborhood shop pays out on a bottle from across town, somebody has to make that shop whole. I'm with {name} until we know who that is.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have the distributors bring a sample claim. We could follow it from that shop to the company writing the check.
author: Codex writer B

text: That money is already out of the till. The store deserves to know who'll pay it back.
author: Codex writer B

text: No clerk can look at a water bottle and tell which route it rode. Settle who pays on the other side of the route first, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd take the clerk out of the route dispute altogether. The delivery companies have the records.
author: Codex writer B

text: What if both distributors send the claim back? The grocer needs somewhere to go with those returned forms.
author: Codex writer B

text: Have the water distributors settle the store's claims together. They can trace their own deliveries after the store gets paid. I'd vote yes, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who puts up the money while those records are being checked? That's what I want settled before the vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put a name and a mailing address on that claim form. I'd take that back to the grocers to see if it answers their question.
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't send someone back across town with an empty water bottle, {presiding}. I'd let the store collect through a common account and start the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which distributors have agreed to put money in that account? I'd ask them to come tell the grocers themselves.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who pays the grocer if the account comes up short? That's the promise I'd want in writing.
author: Codex writer B
